context_facts.fact: Maxwell Street first appeared on Chicago maps in 1847 as a wooden plank road running west from the south branch of the Chicago River to Blue Island Avenue.
The earliest housing in the area was built by and for Irish immigrants brought to Chicago to construct the first railroads.

Beginning in the 1880s, Eastern European Jewish immigrants became the dominant group in the neighborhood, which stayed predominantly Jewish until the 1920s, giving the market its long association with Jewish peddlers and merchants.
The open-air market was officially recognized by the City of Chicago in 1912, and vendors there sold almost anything, new or secondhand, legal and illegal.

From the 1930s-40s, African American musicians performing on Maxwell Street began using amplifiers and electric instruments to be heard over the market noise, a key step in the development of electrified Chicago blues.
In 1994 the City of Chicago moved the Maxwell Street Market to accommodate the expansion of the University of Illinois at Chicago; the market was relocated again, to Des Plaines Avenue, in 2008.
The Library of Congress's 1941 Maxwell Street negatives (LC-USF33-012984 / 012985) were made by FSA/OWI photographer Russell Lee and carry the rights note: "No known restrictions."
